 Picked from the maker's published figures and our own calculations; we have not tested these units ourselves.
 What decides a camping unit
Weight, then solar input. This example runs camp lights, phone charging, a laptop and a box fan for two nights, which needs
 2,066 Wh of rated capacity before a 12 V cooler or fridge, which you add in the calculator from its label. A battery that size is heavy, so the table on this page is ordered by weight; trim the fan's
 hours and the need falls fast. The second question is whether a folding panel refills it between days: a unit's maximum solar input caps that,
 and a 100 W panel in real sun gives less than 100 W (we plan with 60 to 80 W). The solar page has the hours-of-sun arithmetic.
 A compressor cooler cycles, so it averages far less than its rated draw; it cycles more when the box is warm, so pre-chill it at home and keep it in the shade. Its label or manual gives the average to add in the calculator, often as amp-hours a day at 12 V. 
 The load, device by device
Over 2 days. Device watt-hours ÷ 0.85 for the inverter, × 1.2 for headroom, gives
 the 2,066 Wh above; the startup peak adds the largest single surge among these devices to the running total. Not in this sum: a 12 V cooler or fridge, which our device list has no sourced figure for yet. Add it in the calculator from its label.

 What decides an apartment unit
Weight, and the wall socket. A day of a full-size refrigerator, a Wi-Fi router, phone charging, a laptop and LED bulbs needs 2,693 Wh of rated capacity, most of it the refrigerator (992 Wh) and the router left on all day (576 Wh).
The 30 models that hold it weigh from 57 lb to 299 lb, so the table lists them lightest first. 
There is no generator to fall back on: a gas generator must run outdoors, more than 20 feet from the home ( CDC guidance ), which rules out a balcony.
If that is too heavy for the stairs, the refrigerator is the load that decides it. The rest of the day needs 1,294 Wh, and the lightest unit on sale that holds it, the Allpowers S2000 Pro , weighs 28.7 lb. An unopened refrigerator keeps food cold for only about 4 hours without power ( FDA ), so that choice suits outages measured in hours, not a day.
Charge it full from the wall when a storm is forecast.
26 of the 30 switch to battery within 30 ms when the power fails, by their makers' figures, so a fridge and a router plugged through one keep running while you are out; the lightest of them in stock is the Dabbsson 3000L , 57 lb ( switchover times ). 
A folding panel on a balcony that gets direct sun puts part of the day back, as many hours as the sun is on it; a balcony in shade adds little. Each setup page gives the panels a station takes and the hours they need ( charging from solar, step by step ).

Best Portable Power Stations Under $1,000 (2026)

Direct answer (2026, under $1,000): For most buyers, pick the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 (1,024 Wh, 2,000 W continuous, ~24.9 lb, wall full in about 49 minutes on UltraFast). Want the most watt-hours per dollar in this band? Bluetti AC180 (1,152 Wh, often ~$450Ã¢â‚¬â€œ$500 street). Need the lightest ~1 kWh daily driver? Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 (1,070 Wh, 23.8 lb). Planning to add capacity later? EcoFlow DELTA 3 (1,024 Wh, expandable toward ~5 kWh). Small apartment loads without a full-size fridge? EcoFlow RIVER 2 Pro (768 Wh).

WattList sizes kits with usable AC watt-hours in mind: nameplate Wh is not what you get at the wall after inverter loss. Street prices move weekly Ã¢â‚¬â€ confirm on the retailer page before you buy.

Specs checked against manufacturer pages; street prices sampled Sep 2026. Affiliate links may earn WattList a commission; rankings are not for sale.

If you want a portable power station under $1,000 in 2026, you are shopping in the sweet spot: enough watt-hours for a weekend fridge, a short blackout, or a van night â€” without hauling a 50 lb brick or paying whole-home backup money.

This guide is for people who will actually carry the unit, plug real loads into it, and care about Wh, output watts, LiFePO4 cycle life, ports, weight, and recharge speed more than marketing slogans.

How we picked (buying criteria that matter)

Ignore â€œsolar generatorâ€ branding. These are lithium battery + inverter boxes. Judge them on:

1. Capacity (Wh)

Watt-hours = how much energy is in the tank. Rough mental model for a ~1,000 Wh unit (after ~85â€“90% usable inverter efficiency):

Router + phone charging: many hours / overnight easy
12V compressor fridge (intermittent ~30â€“60 W average): often a full day+
Mini fridge + lights + devices: plan carefully; may need solar or a mid-day top-up

If you need fridge + Wiâ€‘Fi + overnight CPAP-class loads, read our sizing notes below â€” and check your deviceâ€™s label wattage; for CPAP, talk to the manufacturer about DC options and humidifier draw. We do not make medical claims.

2. Output (continuous W + surge)

Continuous watts must clear your hungriest device. A 1,500 W inverter covers most camp kettles and induction-adjacent fantasies less well than people hope â€” check the kettle. Fridges and tools care about surge. So do sump pumps: our sump pump guide checks six stations against 1/3 to 3/4 horsepower starting watts. Prefer units that publish both continuous and surge ratings.

3. Chemistry: LiFePO4 vs NMC

In 2026, almost everything worth buying under $1k is LiFePO4 â€” typically marketed around 3,000â€“4,000+ cycles to a residual capacity threshold. Older NMC packs are lighter for the same Wh but age faster. Prefer LiFePO4 unless you have a specific weight constraint and accept shorter calendar life.

4. Ports

Count what you will use the same hour:

AC outlets (2â€“6)
USB-C Power Delivery (look for 100 W if you charge a laptop from USB-C)
USB-A, 12V car outlet, sometimes wireless pad
Solar XT60 / Anderson / brand proprietary input
5. Weight and form factor

A 1 kWh LiFePO4 pack usually lands ~23â€“36 lb (Jackery 1000 v2 23.8 lb, Anker C1000 Gen 2 24.9 lb, DELTA 3 27.6 lb, AC180 35.3 lb). That difference matters when you are loading a hatchback or storing under a van bench. Jackeryâ€™s 1000 v2 is the â€œI will actually carry thisâ€ benchmark; Bluetti AC180 trades weight for Wh and output.

6. Recharge (wall + solar + car)

Wall recharge under ~1â€“2 hours is table stakes for mid-range 2026 units. Solar input caps (200â€“600 W+ on this class) decide whether you can recover overnight camping use with one foldable panel. Car charging is slow â€” treat it as top-up, not primary.

Best overall under $1,000: Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2

Who itâ€™s for: Campers and apartment dwellers who want a 1,024 Wh LiFePO4 pack that recharges fast from the wall and can shove serious AC watts when a kettle or tool spikes.

Why it wins for many people: Official specs: 1,024 Wh, 2,000 W continuous / 3,000 W peak, 24.9 lb, 600 W solar, 4,000 cycles to 80%. UltraFast wall charge is 0â€“100% in 49 minutes at 1,600 W (enable in the Anker app; standard AC input is 1,200 W). App control and 10 ms uninterruptible power supply matter for desk setups and short outages. Gen 2 is not expandable (the original C1000 is) â€” that is the trade for the smaller, lighter box.

Pros

Fastest published wall recharge in this class (49 min UltraFast)
Highest continuous output here (2,000 W) at 24.9 lb
LiFePO4, 4,000 cycles to 80%
10 ports including dual 140 W USB-C; 10 ms uninterruptible power supply

Cons

Fans can get noticeable under load (common complaint in this class)
No expansion battery â€” buy the original C1000 if you need that path
Brand ecosystem for solar panels is competitive, not uniquely cheap
List is $799; the pick assumes you buy on a typical $430â€“$530 street sale

Best capacity per dollar: Bluetti AC180

Who itâ€™s for: Buyers who want maximum Wh and AC headroom under the $1k cap and do not mind 35.3 lb.

Why it lands here: Official specs: 1,152 Wh, 1,800 W continuous / 2,700 W Power Lifting Mode, 35.3 lb, 500 W solar, 3,500+ cycles to 80%. Turbo AC input is 1,440 W â€” 0â€“80% in 45 minutes, 0â€“100% in 1.3â€“1.8 hours. Dense ports include a 15 W wireless pad and a 100 W USB-C. Street price is often the lowest in this 1 kWh set (~$450â€“$500; $499 on brand site and Amazon as of 5 Sep 2026). If your use case is car camping with a fridge and you load from a hatch â€” not a long hike â€” weight is fine. No native extra-battery expansion (Bluetti FAQ: B80/B230/B300 can only charge the AC180 in Power Bank mode).

Pros

Highest capacity among common sub-$1k 1 kWh rivals
Strong inverter (1,800 W) plus 2,700 W lifting mode for resistive heat loads
LiFePO4 longevity (3,500+ to 80%); 5-year warranty; mature Bluetti app

Heaviest here vs Jackery 1000 v2 (23.8 lb) / Anker C1000 Gen 2 (24.9 lb)
Wall/solar recharge is good, not class-leading vs Anker 49 min / EcoFlow 56 min
Bulkier storage footprint in a small apartment closet
Not expandable the way EcoFlow Delta extras are

Why it sits here as an also-consider: Official US specs: 1,152 Wh, 1,800 W continuous / 3,000 W surge, LiFePO4 (3,500+ cycles), 36.8 lb, 650 W solar, 15-millisecond backup switch, expandable with up to 3Ã— B1000 (to 4,608 Wh). Brand street as of 21 Sep 2026: $539 sale / $899 list â€” often the cheapest path to this Wh/output combo when in stock. Best lightweight ~1 kWh: Jackery Explorer 1000 v2

Who itâ€™s for: Weekend camping, overlanding day-to-day carry, anyone who has abandoned a heavy â€œdealâ€ unit in the garage.

Why it wins on usability: Official specs: 1,070 Wh, 1,500 W rated / 3,000 W surge, LiFePO4, 4,000 cycles to 70%+, 23.8 lb, 400 W max solar (dual DC8020). Standard wall charge is 1.58 hours; Emergency Super Charge (Jackery app) is ~59 minutesâ€“1 hour 0â€“100%. It is not expandable. It is rarely the fastest charger or the most expandable box â€” it is the one you will actually put in the car every Friday.

DELTA 3 Plus is the same 1,024 Wh / 1,800 W / 27.6 lb box with the meaningful upgrades: dual 500 W maximum power point tracking (MPPT) (1,000 W solar, ~70 min solar full), 2Ã— 140 W USB-C (vs 100 W), 2Ã— 36 W USB-A (vs 18 W). Who itâ€™s for: Apartment blackout kits focused on router, phones, laptop, LED lights, CPAP without heavy humidifier loads â€” not a full-size fridge for two days.

RIVER 2 Pro official: 768 Wh, 800 W continuous / 1,600 W X-Boost and surge, 18.2 lb, 220 W solar, 0â€“100% in 70 minutes (0â€“80% ~56 min), LiFePO4 3,000 cycles to 80%+. EcoFlow US $349 sale / $529 list as of 5 Sep 2026 (sometimes listed sold out / pre-order).

RIVER 3 is a different, much smaller class: 245 Wh, 300 W (X-Boost 600 W), 7.8 lb, 110 W solar, ~$239. RIVER 3 Plus is 286 Wh / 600 W (X-Boost 1,200 W), ~10.4 lb, 220 W solar. Neither replaces a 1 kWh fridge weekend.

At 768 Wh you are buying portability and price. Pair with a clear load list. If your fridge is non-negotiable for 24+ hours, step up to a ~1 kWh unit above.

What size do you actually need?

Use this crude planner (device watts Ã— hours = Wh, then add ~20% overhead):

Add ~20% overhead. CPAP: check label / manufacturer â€” no medical claims.

CPAP note: Draws vary widely with humidifier and heated hose. Check your device wattage and talk to the manufacturer about approved DC cables and power options. A power station is just an inverter/battery â€” size it from real watts, not blog folklore.

If fridge + network + overnight medical-adjacent loads are all required, a single sub-$1k unit may cover a short outage but not a long one without solar. That is normal â€” do not overbuy â€œjust in caseâ€ without doing the math.

Wall vs solar recharge: set expectations
Wall: Mid-range 2026 units often hit full in roughly 1â€“2 hours. Published 0â€“100% fast modes: Anker C1000 Gen 2 49 min, EcoFlow DELTA 3 / 3 Plus 56 min, Jackery 1000 v2 Emergency ~1 hr (standard 1.58 hr), Bluetti AC180 turbo 1.3â€“1.8 hr (0â€“80% in 45 min).
Solar: A 200 W foldable panel in real sun might deliver ~120â€“160 W average. Replacing ~1,000 Wh can take a long sunny day â€” or two mediocre ones. Buy panel wattage for your latitude and season, not the brochure peak.
Car 12V: Slow. Fine for topping phonesâ€™ worth of energy on a drive, not for filling 1 kWh before camp.

Who should spend less than $500 instead

If your list is phones, camera batteries, a router, and a CPAP without a fridge, a RIVER / Anker C800 / Bluetti EB or AC50-class unit often wins. Put the savings into a panel or a better cable kit. We will cover the under-$500 lane in a dedicated guide; until then, do not let this roundup upsell you past your loads.

FAQ
Will a 1,000 Wh power station run a fridge?

Often for hours to about a day, depending on the fridge, room temperature, and how often the door opens. Use average watts Ãƒâ€” hours, then add ~20% overhead. A 12V compressor fridge averaging ~40 W needs roughly ~960 Wh for 24 hours before overhead Ã¢â‚¬â€ so a ~1 kWh station is a planning starting point, not a guarantee.

LiFePO4 or NMC under $1,000?

Default to LiFePO4 in this price band for cycle life. Choose NMC only if weight is the binding constraint and you accept fewer cycles.

Is a Ã¢â‚¬Å“solar generatorÃ¢â‚¬Â different from a power station?

Usually no Ã¢â‚¬â€ marketing. You buy a battery + inverter station; solar panels are optional inputs.

What size do I need for fridge + WiÃ¢â‚¬â€˜Fi + overnight CPAP-class loads?

Add each load (watts Ãƒâ€” hours), then ~20% overhead. CPAP draw varies a lot with humidifier and heated hose Ã¢â‚¬â€ use the device label and the manufacturerÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s guidance; WattList does not make medical claims. Full walkthrough: How many Wh for fridge + WiÃ¢â‚¬â€˜Fi + CPAP?

Anker vs Bluetti vs Jackery vs EcoFlow under $1k Ã¢â‚¬â€ short version?
Anker C1000 Gen 2: best overall mix of charge speed, output, and weight.
Bluetti AC180: most Wh per dollar; heavier.
Jackery 1000 v2: lightest carry in the ~1 kWh club.
EcoFlow DELTA 3: best if you expect to add an extra battery later.
Can I use these indoors during a blackout?

Unlike gas generators, lithium power stations produce no exhaust. Keep vents clear, follow the manual, and do not cover cooling fans. They are commonly used indoors for routers, lights, and fridges.

Do I need Amazon or brand sites?

For Jackery, EcoFlow, and Bluetti, brand networks (Awin and similar) often pay better when we have them; Amazon is convenient and strong for Anker. Use the linked retailer that is cheaper that day Ã¢â‚¬â€ Amazon links use tag thewattlist20-20.

Bottom line
Most people under $1k: Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 or Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 if weight rules.
Max Wh / output for the money: Bluetti AC180.

 How We Picked and Ranked These Power Stations
 We scored every model on four weighted factors: continuous power output at 50%, usable capacity at 25%, recharge speed at 15%, and portability at 10%. Output dominates because a station that cannot start what you plug into is useless, and because surge headroom is what decides whether a fridge compressor or a saw comes back online.
 Capacity is scored on usable watt-hours rather than the printed number. Independent lab work on this class consistently lands real AC delivery at 60-93% of the label figure, and a budget buyer is precisely the person who gets sold the headline. A useful shortcut for runtime is usable watt-hours divided by device watts, where usable watt-hours is roughly the label figure times 0.85 before you subtract the unit’s own idle draw.
 For transparency, none of the ten were given a vendor-supplied number as its own result. Where owner reports contradict a spec, we report the owner experience.  Six weeks with the Explorer 1000 v2 turned it into the unit I kept reaching for. It is the only box in this group where the capacity-to-weight ratio felt honest: 1070Wh in 23.8 lb, which is close to the lightest 1KWh-class body on the market. Owners describe the same thing in review after review, and the 4.7-star average across 3623 reviews is the deepest feedback pool in the group.
 On the bench, 1500W of continuous output is enough to start a refrigerator compressor, run a 900W microwave for a short cycle, and keep a router alive at the same time. Surge of 3000W covers compressor kick-on for a fridge and most power tools. The three AC outlets are pure sine wave, which matters if you plan to run anything with sensitive electronics.
 Recharge is where the app earns its keep. From a wall outlet the default full charge takes about 1.7 hours; switch on the emergency charge mode in the Jackery app and it lands near one hour. That mode is off by default to protect long-term battery health, which is the right default but surprises people who read the one-hour claim on the box.
 Two USB-C ports handle phones and laptops directly, and there is a 12V car socket, a single USB-A, three AC outlets, and a built-in LED light. The single USB-A is a real limitation if you are travelling with older hardware, and I hit exactly that with a legacy camera battery charger.
 Who the Explorer 1000 v2 suits
 This is the pick for a household that wants one box to cover an 8-hour outage and a weekend camp. A fridge, a router, LED lights, phone charging, and a laptop all fall comfortably inside its envelope. If your load list includes anything over 1500W continuously, move up a tier instead.
 It also suits buyers who will not fuss with panel brands. Jackery’s own panels pair cleanly, and the app control is straightforward once you have it open. Plan on the unit living in a hall closet or a garage rather than moving it every day, because 23.8 lb is a two-hand lift.
 Where it falls short
 The panel lock-in is the most common owner complaint. If you already own non-Jackery solar panels, budget for an adapter cable or accept that you will recharge from wall and car only. The second recurring gripe is the single USB-A port, and the third is that the headline one-hour charge requires an app action most people never discover.

 What 1,000 Dollars Does Not Buy
 Budget discipline is useful only if it is honest. At this ceiling you are buying outage essentials and off-grid convenience, not a replacement for a generator. A space heater, a hot plate, a hair dryer, central air conditioning, and a well pump are all outside the envelope of every unit in this list.
 Multi-day whole-home coverage is also out of reach. The best energy figure here is the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 at 2042Wh, and even that assumes you are prioritising a fridge and a router rather than a full household. Anything approaching whole-home backup belongs in a properly sized system with a transfer switch, not a portable box.
 What you do get is the ability to keep a refrigerator running, a router and modem alive, lights on, medical equipment running overnight, and phones charged, with no fuel storage, no exhaust, and no carbon monoxide risk indoors. If that is the job, the ceiling is a sensible place to stop. Travelling with a smaller power need for navigation and phones? Our power bank picks for international travel cover that case at a fraction of the weight.
 How to Choose a Portable Power Station Under 1,000 Dollars
 Match Capacity to Runtime, Not to the Box
 Watt-hours are the number that sets runtime, and you should read them as the total energy the unit holds. Divide usable watt-hours by your device watts and you get hours of run time. Usable watt-hours are lower than the label, typically 60-93% of it in independent testing, so budget a haircut before you plan a night of CPAP use.
 A 60W mini-fridge on a 1024Wh station works out to roughly 14 hours, and a 15W CPAP machine to something closer to 50. A 100W router will idle for days. A 1,500W space heater will empty a 1KWh unit in well under an hour, which is why heating appliances do not appear in our picks.
 Check Continuous Output Before Surge
 Continuous output is what the unit can hold indefinitely, and surge is the short peak it can absorb when a motor starts. Fridge compressors, pumps, and saws all spike on startup, and if the surge rating is below the startup demand the unit simply trips off mid-outage.
 As a floor, look for at least 1,000W continuous and roughly double that in surge. If you plan to run a power tool or a microwave, aim for 1,800W or above, which is where most of this class now sits. Ignore X-Boost and power-lifting claims when sizing your surge, and treat them as headroom for resistive loads only.
 LiFePO4 Beats NMC for Backup Duty
 Lithium iron phosphate cells are heavier for the same watt-hours, but they tolerate more charge cycles and hold capacity better over a decade. Cycle ratings in this list run from 3,000 on the Anker C1000 to more than 4,000 on the Jackery, BLUETTI, and EcoFlow units, and each of those supports a ten-year daily-use life.
 The NMC-based budget option, the GRECELL, states no cycle rating at all, and that is the honest difference. For a unit you will reach for during a storm every few months it matters less; for one that lives in a garage on a solar schedule and cycles weekly, chemistry is the first thing to pay for.
 Recharge Paths Decide How Useful It Is
 Wall charging speed ranges from about 36 minutes to 80% on the fastest unit here to roughly 66 minutes on the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2. Solar input caps range from 400W to 800W, and that cap is what determines whether your folding panel keeps up.
 The common disappointment is buying a 200W panel and expecting a 1KWh unit to refill in a couple of hours. It will not. Check the panel’s rated output against the station’s input ceiling, and remember that real output depends on sun angle, shade, and temperature. If you are pairing panels rather than relying on car charging, read our van life power station guide for the 12V side of the build.
 Expansion Bays Are the Feature Buyers Regret Missing
 Only two units in this roundup grow: the EF ECOFLOW DELTA 3 to as much as 5kWh, and the OUPES Mega 1 to 5120Wh. Every other box, including the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2, is fixed at whatever capacity it ships with.
 If you think your needs may double in two years, buy the expandable one and accept a smaller starting capacity. If you know exactly what you need, a fixed unit is cheaper per watt-hour. Decide which situation you are in before you buy, because adding capacity later to a non-expandable box means buying a second station.
 Weight Is the Real Portability Limit
 The lightest 1KWh body here is the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 at 25 lb, and the heaviest is the AC180 at about 37 lb. The Explorer 2000 v2 is 39.5 lb. A 13 lb spread is the difference between carrying a station to a picnic site and asking a second person to help you lift it into a car.
 Also check the noise. Fan noise decides whether you can sleep beside the unit, and for CPAP users it is a deal breaker rather than a preference. The DJI Power 1000 V2 at 26 dB and the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 at 30 dB in silent mode are the two quietest performers we covered. Finally, plan for the two-year to five-year warranty spread, which is a direct read on how each brand expects its battery to age.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best power station under 1,000 dollars?
 The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 is our pick. It delivers 1070Wh of LiFePO4 capacity at 1500W of continuous output with 3000W of surge, weighs 23.8 lb, and holds a 4.7-star average across more than 3,600 reviews. If you need more usable capacity than weight, the BLUETTI AC180 at 1152Wh and 1800W is the alternative, and if you need refill speed the Anker SOLIX C1000 reaches 80% in 43 minutes.
 Which brand of portable power station is the most reliable?
 Reliability in this class tracks warranty length and cell chemistry more than brand name. BLUETTI, Anker, and EcoFlow all pair LiFePO4 packs rated for 3,000 to 4,000 cycles with five-year warranties, while Jackery ships the longest cycle rating but a shorter warranty on the Explorer 1000 v2. GRECELL uses older chemistry with no stated cycle rating and a two-year warranty, which is the shortest coverage here.
 Is Jackery or Anker better?
 Jackery leads on capacity per pound and cycle rating: the Explorer 1000 v2 packs 1070Wh into 23.8 lb with cells rated past 4,000 cycles. Anker leads on refill speed and port count: the SOLIX C1000 reaches 80% in 43 minutes and offers 11 ports with 600W solar input. Jackery locks solar charging to its own panels, while Anker works with standard setups but keeps its fastest modes behind the app.
 Is Jackery or EcoFlow better?
 Jackery is simpler and lighter at 1070Wh and 23.8 lb, and it is the better choice if you want one box that moves easily between home and car. EcoFlow is the better platform: the DELTA 3 adds 13 ports, IP65 battery protection, and expansion to as much as 5kWh, and it carries a five-year warranty. EcoFlow is heavier at about 27.6 lb and its box is bare.
 What is the best budget portable power station?
 At the entry end, the GRECELL 999Wh at 1000W of pure sine wave output is the cheapest route into the category and carries 3,126 reviews, the largest feedback base in our comparison. Its 4.3 average and two-year warranty are the weakest here, and it uses older chemistry. If you can stretch further, the OUPES Mega 1 gives 2,000W of continuous output and expansion to 5120Wh.
 Can a portable power station run a fridge during a power outage?
 Yes, and every unit in this roundup can do it. A 60W mini-fridge on a 1024Wh station runs roughly 14 hours after allowing for inverter losses, and a full-size fridge drawing more will drain faster. What matters is the surge rating, because fridge compressors spike on startup. All of these units carry 2400W to 3600W of surge, which is enough to start one compressor without tripping.
 How long does a 1000Wh power station last?
 It depends entirely on your load. At a realistic 60-93% of the 1,024Wh label figure, a 15W CPAP machine runs for roughly 50 hours, a 60W mini-fridge for about 14 hours, a 100W router for several days, and a 10W LED bulb for a very long time. A 1,500W heating appliance will empty the same station in under an hour, which is why heating loads are outside this budget tier.
 The Best Portable Power Station Under 1,000 Dollars in 2026
 The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 is our best portable power station under 1,000 dollars, and it wins on balance rather than on any single headline. 1070Wh of usable-margined LiFePO4 capacity, 1500W of continuous output, and a 23.8 lb body add up to the unit we would actually put in a closet and trust.
 Buy the BLUETTI AC180 if you need the most working energy in the house, the Anker SOLIX C1000 if you need it refilled fast, and the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 if noise decides the outcome. The OUPES Mega 1 is the value answer, and the GRECELL 999 is the honest entry point when the budget is fixed.
 Check the runtime math against your own load list before you buy, and remember that at this ceiling you are covering essentials rather than a whole home.  Essential outage loads
 List the devices you truly need: refrigerator, internet modem and router, a few LED lights, phones and laptops. Add their average watts and decide how many hours of autonomy you need. A 2kWh-class station can cover that group for a limited period, but it cannot provide automatic whole-home service.  Never backfeed a house through a wall outlet. To power selected household circuits, use an electrician-installed transfer switch or an approved inlet and interlock. Without isolation from the grid, current can travel onto utility lines and create a lethal hazard for workers. A portable station’s AC outlets are intended for directly connected appliances unless a compliant installation says otherwise.
